s: a seven-league boot (one of a pair of boots enabling the wearer to cross seven leagues at one stride)
Siebenmeilenstiefel.et: From sieben (“seven”) + Meilen (“miles”) + Stiefel (“boots”). In the German-speaking countries a mile was about 7.5 km (thus roughly 5 international miles).

s: seven (numerical value represented by the Arabic numeral 7; or describing a set with seven elements)
sieben.et:
From Middle High German siben, from Old High German sibun, from Proto-West Germanic *sebun, from Proto-Germanic *sebun, from earlier Proto-Germanic *sebunt, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
Compare Dutch zeven, English seven.

sieben.et: From Middle High German siben or sieben, likely from Old High German sib (“a sieve”). By surface analysis, Sieb + -en.

siebzehn.et: From Middle High German sibenzehen, from Old High German sibunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun. Equivalent to sieben + zehn. Compare Dutch zeventien, West Frisian santjin, English seventeen, Danish sytten.

siebzig.et: From Middle High German sibenzec, from Old High German sibunzug, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntēhundą. Equivalent to sieben + -zig. Cognate with Hunsrik sibzich.

s: sieve; sifter; strainer; colander; riddle (any device with holes used to separate solids from liquids or fine matter from coarse matter)
Wie kann man Wasser in einem Sieb tragen?
How can you carry water in a sieve?
Sieb.et: From Middle High German sip, from Old High German sib, from Proto-West Germanic *sibi. Cognate with Dutch zeef, English sieve.

s: Transylvania (a historical region in western Romania)
Siebenbürgen.et: From sieben (“seven”) + Burg (“fortress”), literally “[in] seven fortresses”.

s: (one of) the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus
sleepyhead, one who sleeps a lot or rises late
Siebenschläfer.et: From Middle High German siben slāfære, referring to the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus. Univerbation since the 15th century. Use for “one who sleeps a lot” since the 17th century. The biological sense since the 18th century because of the animal's hibernation, whic…

Siebenschläfertag.et: sieben (“seven”) + schlafen (“sleep”) + Tag (“day”) or Siebenschläfer (“edible dormouse”) + Tag (“day”)

siebte.et: Syncope of siebente, from Middle High German sibente, sibende, from Old High German sibunto, from Proto-West Germanic *sebundō, from Proto-Germanic *sebundô. Equivalent to sieben + -te.

s: luggage; tools (items carried around e.g. when travelling)
Siebensachen.et: Univerbation of sieben + Sachen. Literally, “seven things”.

s: something with a number, value or size of seven
having seven sides and seven angles, heptagonal
having seventeen sides and seventeen angles; heptadecagonal
a polygon that has seventy vertices and seventy edges; a seventy-sided polygon
Das Boot hatte eine siebenköpfige Mannschaft.
The boat had a crew of seven.

Siebenkampf.et: sieben + Kampf; calque of Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”) + ἆθλον (âthlon, “contest”)

s: ethmoid bone (bone of the skull between the eyes and at the roof of the nose)
Ein Siebenundzwanzigeck ist ein siebenundzwanzigeckiges Vieleck.
An icosiheptagon is a twenty-seven-sided polygon.

siebtjüngst.et: From siebte + jung, with jung put into the superlative form jüngst.

siebtältest.et: From siebte + alt, with alt put into the superlative form ältest.

s: a seven-year-old (male or of unspecified gender)
a seventeen-year-old (male or of unspecified gender)
a twenty-seven-year-old (male or of unspecified gender)
a thirty-seven-year-old (male or of unspecified gender)
Any of several smaller places in Poland and Czechia
Siebenhuben.et: By surface analysis, sieben (“seven”) + Huben (“historical land unit”).

s: a native or inhabitant of Siebenhuben
a native or inhabitant of Siebenbürgen
